utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, the usual question. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can indeed follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Oric. We're joined by our legal assistants, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts. Good morning to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. So, one small announcement before I ask for preliminaries. Due to the need of one of us to travel a bit early today, to travel today, we need to stop not later than 1.00. So what I'm going to suggest is to adopt the same procedure that we have adopted in the past when this has happened, that we have two sessions, rather than three, and that there would be a 30-minute break between the two. The first session will finish at 10.45 instead of at 10.30. We'll recommence at 11.15 and then finish at 1.00, if that is all right with you. The understanding is, Mr. Jones, if you don't finish, we'll spill over to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I anticipate I should be able to finish in any event. But thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that -- and we would find a solution between Monday and Tuesday, if the Prosecution is prejudiced by that, but I don't think it will be prejudiced. So we will spill over to Monday, if necessary. Any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Just to say that yesterday we spotted on the exhibit list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is something that certainly doesn't need any apologies, Mr. Jones. And I also wish to express the gratitude of the Trial Chamber at the positive response that you both showed yesterday in the wake of the memo that one of our legal officers communicated to you with regard to making available as early as possible the list of witnesses because it was causing quite an inconvenience to our staff. But I appreciate your cooperation very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. Please make yourself comfortable so that we don't lose much time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to continue testifying today, and you don't need to repeat the solemn declaration. It still applies, and will continue to apply until the end of your testimony in this Tribunal. So, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Jones: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning again from me, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, you were describing how -- I think it was on the morning of the 5th October 1992 - and correct me if I misstate any of this - you and Sefik Mandzic and your men set off for Joseva in a and Jagodnja because you heard those villages were attacked and on fire. Is that a correct summary of what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, and again I think you stated yesterday, but specifically that those villages had been attacked by Serbs in Fakovici. That's what you told us. I think it's pages 82 to 83.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that you received information that some of the Muslim civilians from those villages had been captured and taken away. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which Serbs did you understand had taken those civilians away?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Serbs from Fakovici, and, later on when I was taken prisoner by the Serbs, there were actually about 200 of us who had been injured, and a guy called Petko Pletvejic [phoen] from Mlecko Obarajka [phoen] boasted to us that he took two Muslim civilians prisoner, Hajro and Osman, that is, and he said that he captured Bahro and a daughter of Mahmut from Joseva, and that she had been sent off to Serbia, and Hajro and Osman are still missing. And a certain Petko, the one I'm talking about, lived at a house in Bratunac. He lived in the house of a well-respected citizen of Bratunac, Hasan Smajlovic, who was a veterinary surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, we're going to come later to when you were taken prisoner. You've told us that Petko boasted that he had taken Muslim civilians prisoner. You mentioned Hajro and Osman. Which villages were they from, or which village?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Poznanovici, and Bahra was from Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind when he told you this, but when he did tell you, when was he saying that he had captured those people?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention any dates as such, but I think it must have been in the course of that period of time, that is to say, October, perhaps August, between August and October, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to Petko later. At the time, and so we're still talking about the 5th of October, 1992, when you were setting off for Joseva and Jagodnja, did you have any information or any belief as to where those Muslim civilians had been taken, those who had been captured?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no information. Our information was that large numbers of Muslims who were on their way to Zanjevo to get food, we had information that quite a few of them were captured, killed, that they stepped in landmines, that a part of Joseva was set on fire and a part of Jagodnja, and -- when Serbs managed to enter that village on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way. You set off with Sefik Mandzic and his group to Joseva and Jagodnja. Part of your information was that Muslim civilians had been taken captive. Was it any part of your intention or not to try and rescue or liberate those captives?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to help. Our intention was to assist the Muslim villages, Jagodnja, and Joseva, to defend themselves against the attack for the villages not to be set on fire, because in Joseva and Jagodnja there were quite a few Muslim refugees from Zanjevo from the direction of Skelani, from Voljavica, from Bjelovac, from Skagari. So our primary intention was to defend that Muslim village, those two Muslim villages, Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, moving on, did you reach Joseva and Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got there at around 2.30, 3.00, across the woods, from Kragljivoda down to Joseva. At around 11.00, and here I'm talking about Boljevici, Radijevici, Gutasa [phoen], Fakovici, and all those places, there were shots being fired in all directions, and also from places across in Serbia. So there was selective shooting and shelling of Muslim villages from all those directions and all those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you say 2.30, 3.00, is that in the morning or in the evening? And what day is that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Actually, what I meant, it took us two and a half hours or three hours to get there, but we reached the place at around 11.00, and it was on the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And you've told us, then, that as you arrived, shots were being fired in all directions, including from Serbia. And here again just to clarify your testimony, you say: "At around 11.00 a.m., there were shots being fired in all directions." Were shots being fired from those places? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. They were shooting from those villages that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you remain in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Other groups had reached Jagodnja before us from Miholjevine, Mosici, a group from Jagodnja and Joseva, the group that was there. They were chasing the Serbs, actually, and shooting after them. And that's how they managed to chase away the Serbs who had come into their village and torched it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then from that point, then, did you go -- where did you go after being in Jagodnja? And you can also indicate on the map, if that helps to show your route. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and just while the map is being produced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the map is already on the ELMO, if I'm seeing right. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know if Mr. Jones intends to clarify it or not. He may, and I apologise if I'm interrupting prematurely. But the witness indicated there were other groups there chasing the Serbs away. I don't know if Mr. Jones intends to lead any evidence of what those groups were or who they were. But if he doesn't, my submission is that there ought to be some clarification of that for you to understand this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I leave that for cross-examination, really. I can't pursue every line which the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is going to force you to pursue that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could show us -- we see Jagodnja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you would understand, Mr. Di Fazio, that being the answer, we are not going to pursue it. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand Mr. Jones' position. I can't quarrel with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you don't quarrel with us, too. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this map, Mr. Buric, can you see Jagodnja and Joseva, the map which is to your right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already circled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for you to locate it. Now, you mentioned shots being fired, well, from -- Fakovici was one place. Let me just check on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fakovici, Boljevici, Gutasa, and Radijevici. So all Serb villages, which are situated along the River Drina, next to the Muslim village Zanjevo Abdulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "shots," was this rifle shots, artillery shells? What sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, before he answers, for the record, the witness has been indicating and circling these places on the map which was exhibited yesterday and which is marked as Defence exhibit 737. Sorry, Mr. Jones. I think we needed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of shots were being fired from these locations?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were using infantry ammunition, guns, machine-guns, mortars, anti-aircraft machine-guns. But we'll get that later. But at around 4.00, tanks rolled up from Serbia, from the direction of Perucac. So then all sorts of artillery weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's quite a bit later. So firstly, did you -- where in fact did you go --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Joseva and Jagodnja? What locations?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to Joseva, a group from Joseva had already pushed Serbs away into the direction of Radijevici and Sefik and myself, with our group -- groups, rather, went in the direction of Radijevici, not far from Joseva, in a forest which was totally land-mined. Sefik stepped on a land-mine, and it was actually an anti-tank mine and it blew him to pieces. But four blokes from his group went to help him and the same fate had befallen them as well. So before we even left Joseva properly, we had five dead. And that was one of the most difficult days in my life, Sefik's death, and he was a great friend of mine. And so most of the group from Kragljivoda was actually busy taking the dead bodies away. And there were quite a few women who had stepped on land-mines, as well as children from Joseva, and they were all being taken in the direction of Joseva and Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to stop you there. The land-mines, or the anti-tank mine, in fact, which Sefik stepped on and which the four others -- which killed the four others, where precisely was that? Was that in any village? What was the closest village to where that happened?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Radijevici halfway between Joseva and Radijevici, roughly speaking here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Radijevici was a Serb or Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an ethnically Serb village, and they were attacking from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that direction and they managed to torch a part of Joseva on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you've marked Radijevici yet on the map, but if you haven't I'd be grateful if you'd do so.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I marked it. There are three big circles and the biggest one indicates Radijevici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. Now, you've told us that Sefik and four blokes died in that area. Was this area lightly mined, heavily mined, moderately mined? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that there were several hundreds of mines. I did say that in the beginning. Whenever Serbs felt that it was appropriate, they would have minefields, everywhere, Fakovici, Radijevici, all that was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is Radijevici from Fakovici, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but five to six kilometres, tops. And in between those two Serb villages, there is a Muslim village, Abdulici Zanjevo that's one village, in fact, which was torched on the 7th or 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So what happened after that? Where did you go after Sefik and the four others had died?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those lads from Kragljivoda went back to Joseva and Jagodnja to get the dead bodies out of there, and with a part of my group, I went to the left, in the direction of the village of Zanjevo. Because I thought that in that way, we could avoid the minefields. So we went to the right of a creek of some sort, between Zanjevo and Fakovici. And at one point, my left eye could see a church. That was the church in Fakovici. So I went to the left and I kept going in that direction and I came near Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you explain that, earlier you mentioned that you also saw women, I think you said children also, who had been wounded. Can you just elaborate that for us, roughly how many women and children and what sort of injuries -- the extent of the injuries that they suffered.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are dozens of women, children, people in general who were being carried either by other people or transported on horseback, and most of them had stepped onto land-mines. So they were going from the direction of Joseva and Jagodnja. So as soon as their group from Joseva and Jagodnja went in the direction of Radijevici, the civilians probably followed, because they must have thought that they were going to get into Radijevici and they followed the groups from Joseva and Jagodnja straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know roughly where they -- where they encountered these mines and where they were injured, in what locality?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the left of that area, so it was in the western part of Fakovici, from the direction of Jagodnja and Joseva. Okay. I've just marked it with a couple of arrows here. So it was between Fakovici and Zanjevo. Because they supposed that Muslims would go back to their own village to get food, to Zanjevo, that is. And 99 per cent of the area was mined. 99 per cent of that Muslim village, Zanjevo Abdulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling us how you had seen the approach and you said you came near Fakovici. At that stage -- firstly, who were you with in your group?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the way to Jagodnja and Joseva, we were joined by some other lads from the refugee settlement of Tokoljaci and some others from Joseva from Jagodnja who also had rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you come in - when I say "you," I'm referring to you and anyone who was in your group approaching Fakovici - did you come under any shooting at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that time, as soon as Jagodnja and Joseva had been set on fire, at some point in the morning - I can't remember what time exactly - but throughout that period of time, until 11.00 or 12.00, there was relentless shooting and shelling from all sorts of weapons, artillery weapons, and it came from this direction of Fakovici. It was to the east and the southeast of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you at any stage know or find out what artillery was shooting at you from Fakovici, what type of artillery?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, we thought these were all guns of sorts. We didn't know the exact categories of weapons. We called all of them guns and rifles until we reached Fakovici, and then we saw what it was that we seized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm anticipating slightly, but what did you seize?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fakovici was so heavily armed and we saw so much weaponry that it was beyond our dreams. We seized a truck, FAP-13, with a three-barrelled gun called P-A-T, PAT, 20-millimetre calibre, as well as a four-barrel gun, three or four mortars of 80-millimetre calibre and five or six of them. Two tractors loaded with ammunition for PAT and PAMs, a quantity of automatic rifles and machine-guns. That was all seized in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to make sure I've got this list absolutely right. A truck with the three-barrel gun on it, which I think you said was 20-millimetre calibre. Dealing with that first of all. Can you describe the truck, including the colour? I'm interested in the colour as well, for my own purposes.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truck was yellow. It was produced at the Privoj factory, the abbreviation being the FAP, and it had a PAT mounted, welded into the chassis. It was a three-barrelled gun with spare ammunition, and it was an anti-aircraft gun of 20-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned -- actually, while we're on that, can you tell us where that was located?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Flak. I will show the exact spot. On the left side of the road between Bratunac and Skelani, just below the road. I will put a dot there. This is where the Flak was, f-l-a-k, a three-barrelled down. And three to four hundred metres down was the four-barrelled gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, just for the sake of the record, could you put maybe a "3" next to the dot you've done to indicate three-barrelled gun.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's within the circle that you've marked "F," so I take it that's within Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's deal with the four-barrelled gun. I'm not sure if you mentioned what calibre that was, but if you tell us the calibre and where that was located.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That four-barrelled gun, I don't know the exact categorisation of the JNA, but it is of 20- or 40-millimetre calibre. I believe it must be 40. It's got four barrels and a crew, and it was about 300 metres down towards the Drina. That's where I put number 4. That was the four-barrelled gun. And in between the houses, there were mortars of 82 and 60-millimetre calibre. And if I may add, there were ramparts and bunkers and dugouts that were made of sandbags and crates, ammunition crates that were filled with earth. The greatest problem that we had was the place that we call salas. It is a place where we keep wheat. And they dug out a trench next to it and put some concrete in as well. And they kept firing from there, in all directions, around Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described this place called salas, where there was a trench. But you've also described ramparts and bunkers and dugouts. Can you tell us where these ramparts and bunkers and dugouts were located in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make myself clear, not one salas, which is actually a barn. It is a regular feature with the outhouses. And there wasn't just one barn, therefore, but each house had its own, and fire was opened from behind each one of the houses. And we knew from before that there used to be a professional battalion of the Serb army in Fakovici and that on occasion they received units from Bratunac, Skelani, and Bijeljina. And we knew that. And at a certain point, and that proved to be true later, they even had cadets from Belgrade who underwent training there. Those cadets attended the military academy and they would come to Fakovici and Skelani for the shooting exercises and combat practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, still remaining with this list of items which were captured, you've described the two -- the three-barrelled gun and the four-barelled gun and the mortars tars as well. You also mentioned ammunition, I think you said PATs, were also seized?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that captured?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was seized around noon or 12.30 on the 5th of October. Just below the road where the three-barrelled gun was - I don't know exactly, because that was the first time and the last time I was in Fakovici - but there is a facility there. I think it's an agriculture cooperative in their warehouse. And when we went in, it was mined. As far as I can remember, a Serb returned to mine the warehouse. And some of our guys saw that and they prevented him to blow up the facility, because it was full of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two questions about that. You said that the agriculture cooperative was mined. But then you mentioned a Serb returned to mine the warehouse. What precisely did you mean by that? What in fact did the Serb who returned, what did he try to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They thought that the Muslim groups would come into the warehouse, would storm into it, and they had laid mines previously. But I suppose they never expected the attack, since they torched Jagodnja and Joseva, they didn't consider the option of a counterattack. And it was probably mined days before that, just in case. And he returned to try to set it off. They waited for us to storm in and then to set it off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he tried to detonate the mine?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to that Serb?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guys from Jagodnja and Joseva took that Serb to Jagodnja and Joseva. I don't know what happened to him afterwards. They captured him and took him to Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, at this point, I'd be grateful if the witness could be shown exhibit D135?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this is a statement taken from someone from Fakovici. Before the witness is shown the exhibit:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the age of this Serb who was captured?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Around 50, I guess. Around 50, 55. That's what he looked like to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll be shown this exhibit now, and it's a statement which was taken from someone from Fakovici, relating to the 5th of October, 1992. And I'll direct you to the fourth paragraph on page 1, I think in both -- yes, in English and in B/C/S. And the bit I'm going to read goes as follows: "When the shooting stopped, I crept behind the arms depot and got to about 30 metres away from them," referring to the [inaudible], "they were trying to break into the warehouse, which had an iron gate. When the gate began to give way, I ran for the detonator, because I knew the warehouse was mined. I wanted all of them to" - I think that's "go in" - "before it blew up. However when I got to within 10 metres, they sprang out of hiding where they were guarding the warehouse. They grabbed me, beat me, and dragged me to my house, which was on fire." I just want to ask if that corresponds to what you were telling us about a Serb on the 5th of October trying to detonate a charge on a warehouse, but getting caught instead.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one beat him, that Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I would just kindly ask the witness to read for himself this part of the text, because the translation is wrong. Could you please read the third paragraph quoted by my colleague, because the witness received a translation that is incorrect and difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That corrects it. And do you want him to read it from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. He can just read it where it starts [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand me, Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can comment. And he mentioned the barn, but he used a different word in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't comment. Just read the paragraph out slowly, from the part that Mr. Jones indicated to you, so that we will have the benefit of a real-time interpretation and we will know what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Going down to line 7 - sorry, 10, the last word should be [B/C/S spoken]. We don't need to go beyond there. Do you want the witness to actually read that passage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so, because if he doesn't read it out, how are we going to find out what the discrepancy is or where the -- where the wrong translation is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, I don't know if you followed that. If you could read -- it's the fourth paragraph, and you could just read out loud where it starts off [B/C/S spoken], and go down nine lines to where it says [B/C/S spoken]. If you could just read that, we need it for the record.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it. "When the weapons became silent, I crept behind the arms depot and I came closer -- close to a barn close to them, about 30 metres away, and they were trying to break into the warehouse that had an iron gate. They were beating on it. And when the gate gave way, I ran to the detonator, because I knew the warehouse was mined. I didn't want to blow it up before that. I wanted for all of them to go in. When I started running, I was about ten metres away from the detonator, and suddenly about a hundred of them appeared. They were hidden and guarding the warehouse from all sides. They encircled me, carried me away, and beat me, put me before my house. They knew who I was, and they said, `here you go, manager.'"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two questions: Firstly, does that description correspond to what your information about a Serb being captured after trying to rob the warehouse of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he said that he came to blow up the warehouse and that it was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question arising from something you said earlier. You see Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there that it says you were beaten. Do you disagree or disagree? And if you disagree, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. No one beat him. Two guys from Jagodnja took him away. They didn't even know him. All we knew was that he was a Serb who came to blow up the warehouse. We didn't know who he was. We never saw him before that. And we didn't take him to his house, because he was immediately taken towards Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's something else in this statement which I'd appreciate your help with. It's the third paragraph. And I'd be grateful if you could just read into the record the last sentence. It's the sentence [B/C/S spoken], if you could read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the moment when they were going down the Drina, our weapons jammed, and only my Zuca was still functioning."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A question about that. What would you understand, if anything, by that reference to Zuca?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We neutralised the Flak before that, and he said that their weapons jammed. Zuca is the three-barrelled gun that was mounted on the truck that was yellow. And it was still -- functioned, and it was seized after we captured him and that was the last place of resistance. He may have been the only person manning it and he went to the warehouse to detonate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I point that out because the English doesn't have the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is often of concern to the Trial Chamber. When we see these things, the discrepancies, or inaccuracies, we really get worried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We received this from the Prosecution. You can see it's receipt 11 to their translation, or at least it's a translation we received, and we pointed this out, I believe, in the past, that those words were missing, I'm pretty sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you need to realise something. I mean, the Defence, the right to remain silent, and I cannot look in the direction of the Defence and say: If there are discrepancies, you are required to point them out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've asked our CaseMap manager to check, because I believe we have pointed this out in the past. We can deal with this in the absence of the witness subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would appreciate, of course, but you realise this causes quite a concern at the back, and we go to bed thinking about these things. Because ultimately, I mean, this is a case where you have almost 800 -- we have 1.300 documents. And some of them -- we rely entirely on the translation that we are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I just refer Your Honours, for future reference, it's 16th of December, 2004, page 67, on LiveNote, 67, 10, when this issue was raised in the context of this exhibit. But I'll try to move on, obviously, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to where we left off, because in fact you haven't described your movements yet in Fakovici. We dealt with what was captured. So I want to go back to your entry into Fakovici. I want to first of all ask whether at that time and that day in Fakovici, whether you saw any civilians, Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before we moved in that direction, Joseva, Radijevici, and towards the left, I saw thousands, perhaps between 5.000 and 10.000 people who have already entered the Muslim village of Zanjevo. So a large number of people was coming back with wheat bags from Fakovici and ambari [as interpreted]. There were masses of civilians, women and men. In my estimate, between 5.000 to 10.000 people. And when I was returning, I believe there were up to 15.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned they were coming back with wheat bags. It may be an obvious question, but why were the civilians in Fakovici, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was going there, I said from the Muslim village of Zanjevo. First we went to the left of Zanjevo, and they have already been coming in, looking for food, wheat, corn, whatever they could find, and then they were returning towards Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described your group who were there, some or all with rifles or with weapons. Were you coordinating and choreographing the movements of these civilians?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'd ask you repeat the question, please, and then we'll see whether it's a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, and by you, I mean you and your group who had weapons, were you coordinating and choreographing the movements of these civilians? Were you directing them where to go and what to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of the people from my group had weapons, but we had no coordination, no links with those civilians. We were not interested in them, and they were not interested in us. People were just trying to reach the barns to get some food. No one was interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And again, maybe an obvious question, but was there any possibility of controlling those people, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was not even the slightest possibility to have any influence over them. No one could. People moved through the woods, since it is a forested area. I am short of words to explain myself, but they came from all directions. They never minded the mines, and when someone would step on a mine, they would have to pull that person out. I believe on that day, several dozens of -- thousands of people died [as interpreted], women, children, and up to 90 per cent of them died because they stepped on mines, and they never even got close to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dozens of thousands? This is what I have in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There might be a mistake in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people did you say in fact you thought had died?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several dozens, 30, 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you said 30, 40, not thousands. That's what I heard in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because like that, it would be -- you know, I am, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It would be the end of the enclave. I have a new exhibit for the witness, 04337002, and this is Bratunac garrison command, strictly confidential, number 243, 12, date 6 October 1992, urgent to Birac Brigade command. And I'm going to read into the record the two -- two paragraphs: "We will engage one aircraft with two air sorties for air operations and we will fulfil other requests. In the enemy attack on Fakovici yesterday, 20 people, soldiers and women, were killed, and one person went missing. The enemy captured two 20-millimetre anti-aircraft guns, a three-barrel and a four-barrel one, three 82-millimetre MB mortars with about 60 shells, an M-84 PM light machine-gun, two M-53 PMs, and about 10 APM."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing there, can you help us with the references to PMs and APM?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An automatic rifle and a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've confirmed the three-barrelled gun and the four-barrelled gun and these mortars. Did you also -- can you also confirm whether you seized or captured any machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. My group captured a machine-gun of 84-millimetre calibre, as well as five or six automatic rifles. That's my group, that is, as well as a three- and a four-barrelled gun, as I mentioned. And I can add: It says here that in the attack, 20 persons were killed. In the house in Fakovici that they used as a bunker, this is the only place where I saw some of their people killed, five or six of them, and this was a house with ramparts, on six or seven different sides, and sandbags. There were six to seven dead there, and we took their automatic rifles and the machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were those men dressed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all wore the JNA olive-drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of this list, firstly, of these captured items, is that, as far as you know, list complete, or was there more or less than what's stated there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we managed to seize five or six times more ammunition. They never mentioned the grenades. So we seized five to six times more of weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you seize that ammunition and also the rifles from purely one location or from more than one location?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. No. On several occasions. They were retreating. Most of them had a way out, a spare route to withdraw towards the Drina, and then they crossed over to Serbia, using a vessel, and that's how they communicated with Serbia proper. Most of their armed forces in Fakovici withdrew to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned these -- I think you said seven, six or seven men who you had seen who were killed. Do you know how they had been killed? Did you see how they appeared to have been killed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could not approach them from any side. They offered resistance for about two to three hours before we got there. So they were offering resistance. They were firing. And we had to use Zoljas and hand-grenades. And so we fired about five of each at that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you fired those weapons to flush them out or to stop them firing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To stop shooting. They could have escaped or withdrew, as the others did, across the River Drina, where several hundreds of Serb soldiers crossed over into Serbia, and those ones didn't want to do so, so that's why they got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to several hundreds of Serb soldiers. What's your best estimate for how many Serb soldiers were fighting in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have the information that in Fakovici there was a military battalion between 3 and 600 soldiers, that's the figure that we presume was accurate. Perhaps a part of them withdrew in the direction of [indiscernible] in the direction of Joseva, perhaps they went to Radijevici. Not all of them to Fakovici. But at least it must have been 300 soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just on the subject again of where you found weapons and ammunition. Did you find any of that in houses, by which I mean private houses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons we found were, most of them, in the house that offered the most resistance. And as to everybody else, it was all in barns, in houses, even in the fields, as they were withdrawing in the direction of the River Drina, they were dropping weapons as they went. And that PAM and PAT that we captured, they actually took off some parts and they dropped them as they were fleeing in the direction of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also referred to the possibility that some soldiers could have withdrawn to Radijevici. I want to read the second paragraph of this exhibit: "Our forces are holding Radijevici village, but other villages, Fakovici, Boljevici, and Grabovicka Rijeka are empty." Now, was that correct, to your knowledge, that the Serbs actually held Radijevici, certainly on the 5th of October, 1992, firstly?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, your group and any other groups which were fighting in Fakovici, did you hold the area? Did you occupy Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., Serbs got help from Perucac and Bajina Basta, where there was transport vehicles and buses and Niva cars and quite a few people came. Whatever moved in Bosnia at Fakovici was destroyed by those tanks. And it's about 2 to 300 metres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on what you mean by that, when you say that whatever moved in Bosnia at Fakovici was destroyed by those tanks? If you could elaborate on what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. - I marked it with an arrow - Serb tanks arrived from Bajina Basta and they were stationed along the road, and they supposed that Muslims, that quite a few Muslim civilians would be in Fakovici and they must be hiding in their houses. And they started selective shelling operation of all buildings. I mean, it can still be seen these days, because the Muslim side never had any artillery weapons. And you can see -- you can still see holes in the walls of the Fakovici houses, and the fire was coming from Serbia. And so on that day, they destroyed everything with their tanks and APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And just to go back to that a little bit, and I don't want you to make any supposition about what the intentions were of the Serbs when they were shelling. What I want to know firstly is, did you see these tanks firing from the other side of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that they, the Serbs, supposed that Muslims, that quite a few Muslim civilians would be in Fakovici, what's your basis for saying that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen with the naked eye. It's only 200 metres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on, I'd like to ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. What's the next number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 740. So this document, which in the original language has ERN number 04337002, with the corresponding translation into English, is being tendered and received and marked as a Defence Exhibit D740.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned APCs firing. Now, an APC, I take it is an armoured personnel carrier. Can you explain how they were shooting from APCs?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The BOV vehicle on tyres, and on top of that vehicle there is a gun, 20- to 40-millimetre gun, and there were two to three such APCs, basically, there that came along with the tanks. So they had smaller guns, lesser-calibre guns. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also mentioned TOP, I heard the word Topovi. Firstly, can you confirm that you mentioned TOP, and let us know what TOP refers to.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the APCs, there is a gun. On top of that, there is a gun which is a 20- to 40-millimetre one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think actually we need to clarify this, because it will come up. I'm referring to TOP, T-O-P. That's an expression in Bosnian and the witness is using the word, and I'd be grateful if the witness could confirm whether or not he's used the word "TOP," T-O-P?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a technical word. What is a top, Mr. Buric? What is a top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. I understand that in the context of what we are discussing, weapons, et cetera, there is a term used in your language which is "TOP." What is a "TOP"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a weapon. It can also be called a PAT anti-aircraft gun, a 20-millimetre gun, and it is called TOP. Perhaps another translation could be a cannon, but "gun" is just as good. So the smallest calibre is mounted onto an APC, such as the anti-aircraft gun which was on a lorry, a four-barrelled one. And the one that only has one barrel is mounted onto an APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it's important to clarify, because "gun" in English is very generic, because a TOP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I do take it, at least I don't know whether you are going to pursue this along the lines of what has been indicated to us, but I see that amongst the Defence exhibit numbers, you intended to make use of, there's generic photos of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you're going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to use that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- it's all right. I'm sorry. I mean, when the time you want to use them, is of course up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. The important thing is that we establish the calibre, and the witness has answered that TOP is a 20-millimetre gun which could also be described as a cannon. That's fine. And the guns on the other side of the Drina, I think you described that it was a 20-millimetre gun mounted on the APCs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Buric, could you repeat your answer, please, because the interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've described the tanks and APCs on the other side of the Drina firing into Fakovici in the afternoon. I want to establish with you as clearly as possible, firstly, how frequently they were firing, and then for how long, to your knowledge, from what you observed.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., when those tanks and APCs came along, I started withdrawing in the direction of a Muslim village called Poznanovici. So we took a truck which had been captured and we also took the Flak weapon that I've mentioned before, and some ammunition. And let me just mention that we had found quite a lot of Muslim property there, the machinery that had been looted from the Muslim villages, Zanjevo, Tegare, Voljevici, so people actually found their own trucks and tractors, et cetera. So they took those tractors of theirs and drove in the direction of Poznanovici. So at around 4.00 p.m., I myself withdrew in the direction of Poznanovici, because that was the only road that was suitable for a tractor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But what I want to explore with you now is the intensity of the shooting which was coming from the other side of the Drina. And if you can just describe in some words what the intensity of the shooting was, the frequency, and the duration.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was travelling in that direction. I set off at some point between 3.00 and 4.00 p.m., and it took me about three hours to get to Poznanovici. And there was unrelenting shooting. There were detonations that we could hear all the time from that direction, from Radijevici, Boljevici, from Serbia, from Nemici. So they had artillery weapons at a distance as well. And from Bratunac. So it was incessant. And those detonations that I could hear clearly lasted for about three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described yesterday how you experienced shelling in Osmace, and you described the damage which it did to property in Osmace. Can you help us with the sort of shelling which you saw in Fakovici, the sort of damage which that can do to property?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, I went back to Fakovici and I saw the houses that had taken direct hits. And they had the so-called Weber [as interpreted] weapons from Nemici. The next day, when I went back to Fakovici, I saw a whole range of damage to Serb houses. Because, I mean, Muslims had no artillery weapons and were in no position to use it, therefore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify another point. In the transcript there's a reference to Weber. I heard you say VBR. Can you confirm what you were referring to, those weapons from Nemici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is multiple rocket launcher. We're talking about rockets of a larger calibre. As to the exact nomenclature, I don't know whether it would be called Plamenflem [phoen], or whatever, or organ, and the range is much longer and they used it from Nemici and Bratunac, from bigger distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has Nemici been indicated on the map, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure it has. It's actually, as the witness says, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think it would be better if we have an indication of where it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not indicated here. It is to the north of Ljubovija. To the north of Ljubovija there is an elevation called Nemic that we were kind of familiar with, and they used that position for the shelling of the entire area along the River Drina around Srebrenica. It's not indicated on the map. But it is -- it's somewhere near Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might be possible to mark it on this other map which we have which has Ljubovija. I'll pass this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Jones. At least we'll have an indication of where Nemici is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map which I'm going to use in discussing Kravica, but we'll distribute it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it's permitted for me to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In these matters, I'm sure that Mr. Di Fazio is not going to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you just go to the right, where your finger is now, Mr. Buric. The other direction. You've got Ljubovija. If you move to the right, you see Nemic Kamen, 797.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Pod Nemic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. And thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is something that could have been seen with the naked eye, as they were shelling from Voljevica. You could see clearly the rockets fired from the multiple rocket launcher, and you could see it clearly from the area of Nemici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us you went back the next day to Fakovici. I want to ask you firstly: Did you see on that day any signs, or the day before, did you see houses that had been -- were being deliberately set on fire? Is that something you saw?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no fires at all. On that day, on the 5th and the 6th, in the morning, when I myself went back to Fakovici, not a single house had been set on fire. 99 per cent of the houses had been totally destroyed and devastating on the basis of this selective shelling from tanks and by the people who went in. But not a single house had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you able to be sure? How were you able to distinguish between a house which has been damaged by shelling and one which has been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any houses which had been burnt in any way. They were devastated. They were destroyed by tanks. But also because roofs were still standing that had been damaged. But if you have a house which has been torched, you can see soot, and it's all black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And could you tell us why you went back the next day to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I got to a point on the road where we got stuck with that lorry carrying a three-barrelled gun, and we couldn't go any further. And we spent the night there, and we got the information according to which many people had been killed and left behind in Fakovici, and that in the evening hours, Serbs crossed over on a barge from Serbia and that there was a whole lot of massacred Muslims who had been left back in Fakovici. So I went, together with my group, about 20 of us, and we were joined by 40 more - roughly speaking - people from Poznanovici. And we tried to go back and get the dead bodies out. So we got a tractor and we prepared to go and we entered Fakovici. There was no resistance whatsoever. And as we entered Fakovici, we were met with a terrible, horrific sight, dead bodies scattered all over the road, around the houses, Muslim bodies. And I could see about 14 Muslim bodies lined along the road, really lined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move those bodies or try to move them?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already knew what Serbs were doing. We know that they played dirty and we knew that the bodies would have been mined. But we prepared for that in advance, because we had ropes. And we hooked the first one on the left and we pulled the rope, and that's how we detonated the mine. And that's what we did, to all bodies, one by one. We started at both ends and actually there were mines at both ends, to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serbs actually had mined these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they did. We loaded them on the tractors and turned back in the direction of Poznanovici. And there was no fight. There was no resistance. During the night, they went in. They did whatever they did, and there was a whole lot of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those bodies you saw, were they in any sort of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those dead bodies of dead Muslims were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it may be suggested to you at some point that fighters in Fakovici distinguished themselves from civilians by using coloured ribbons so they could notice each other. What would you say to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was involved as well, and I was wearing no ribbon at all. And nobody else in the group of people who were with me. And we're talking about several dozens of people. Nobody had any ribbons or anything like that, or any marking of any other sort. They were civilians. The only thing is that certain individuals carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And also just as a slight digression, I want to ask you a bit about mines, and this is based on your experience of the war in Bosnia. Can anyone lay land-mines, or is that something which requires professional training?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim with a great deal of responsibility that in my group or, as you call it, unit, in March 1993, nobody knew how to plant a mine. And it was as late as March 1993. This is just to say that you have to go through a special training in order to do that. You have to be a technical expert. In order to plant a mine under a dead body, you have be exceptionally skilled. I really don't know what's kinds of mines they have to be, but I do know for certain that you have to be specially trained for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've referred to civilians being present in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992. Do you know how the civilians knew to be in Fakovici on that day or why they came to be there when you were also there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all spontaneous, as it were. Civilians from nearby villages, Jagodnja and Joseva, had large numbers of refugees, and as soon as they realised that some groups, people, were moving in the direction of Zanjevo. They went after them. So this is a movement of people that went on for hours, for days, in fact. People from all the surrounding villages, as soon as they heard shooting, they would just follow, go with the flow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact civilians would head for places where there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how much food was captured in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that so much food was found in Zanjevo, and I'm referring to the Muslim village, Zanjevo, Abdulici Fakovici, and there was so much food that for days, for months, in fact, people went back and took that food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm leaving the subject of Fakovici now, but we have another 15 minutes, so I'll move on to the next area. There's no need to dwell on the food crisis at any length. It's something which Their Honours have indicated they've heard sufficient evidence on. But I would like, just for us to have a flavour, for you to describe for us any examples which come to mind of the state of the food crisis after Fakovici and before December 1992.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since a number of refugees, civilians, and children from the area was great, because, as we said, in May and in June, all Muslim villages along the Drina were torched, towards Bratunac, there were so many people, probably around 50.000 people in a small area, and Srebrenica being a mountainous terrain, there was not enough food and nowhere to buy it. So whatever could be found, say 20 kilometres [as interpreted] of wheat meant food for five to six days. And everything was based on wheat and corn. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And because of the shelling that went on on a daily basis, it was very difficult. And the Serbs began using stronger and stronger artillery and daily sorties by planes that would take off from Bratunac or from Ponikve in Serbia proper, and those were MiGs. And the convoys didn't come through. The Serbs in Bratunac didn't allow for convoys to pass. I believe there was one in November. Otherwise, they wouldn't let any convoy go through to Srebrenica. And just to add, if I may: Someone took the cartridges [as interpreted] to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said there was general chaos in Srebrenica. Is that something which you said?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. In Srebrenica in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 20 kilogrammes of wheat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I would take it it's 20 kilogrammes and not kilometres. The other thing is someone took -- the line, page 37, line 1, Mr. Jones, says someone took cartridges to Belgrade. I would imagine he meant someone diverted the carriages to Belgrade, not cartridges. We're not talking of cartridges here. We're talking of food supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what you were referring to in relation to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Someone from higher up, all those humanitarian organisations that delivered food to Bosnia-Herzegovina, transferred their operation to Belgrade, and we know all too well what Belgrade did to Bosnia and Herzegovina in this war. So a convoy would come from Belgrade to Srebrenica. So at any pointed, Serbs could stop it, either at the bridge in Ljubovija or at the yellow bridge in Bratunac. It never reached Srebrenica. So people were starving to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just on a couple of other issues in relation to this. Obviously we're talking about Muslim civilians. Do you know if people ever actually ate pork, despite the taboo or the prohibition on eating pork?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw personally that Muslims didn't eat pork, and they wouldn't eat it at any cost [as interpreted]. What I saw in Fakovici was that they were killing pigs in order to survive. So that was the extent of the famine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, they would eat pork?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- you're familiar, I take it, with Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people from Zepa ever come to Srebrenica in this period, October to December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility, Your Honours, that people would come to Fakovici for days, up to 100 people with horses from Krusev Dol, via forests, they came to get just one kilogramme of wheat. And dozens of them died around Fakovici, and in Fakovici itself, but it was all an attempt to get some food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And also, you've told us how a warehouse in Fakovici was mined. You've described how dead bodies were mined. In sorties by civilians to get food outside Srebrenica, did that pose a problem of buildings being mined, to your -- in your personal experience, if you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't interested in whether anything was mined that's why there were a lot killed. And people often died on their way to Serb barns. Thousands of them left their lives there. They never asked anyone. They weren't careful. I went to an area where some people from my village went to get some food, and the Serbs were living there still. But irrespective of that, they went down there and the Serbs captured them and killed them by those barns, and those bodies were never retrieved and buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing. You said that thousands of people lost their lives. Are you saying literally thousands of people died in getting food or are you being somewhat hyperbolic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are talking about the wider region of Srebrenica. In March of 19 -- up until March 1993, about three and a half thousand people died. The list of the dead and the missing from Srebrenica amounts to twelve and a half thousand, between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us what you were actually doing in late 1992, October to December 1992. You've told us before you were in Osmace. Were you still in Osmace in that period?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shelling on a daily basis, people starving to death, as well as aviation strikes by the Serb forces. And I was in Osmace throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any sort of pattern to bombings -- sorry. You've referred to aviation strikes. Was there any pattern that you could discern in those strikes?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs had a goal, and they did have a list of sorts of extremist Muslim villages, and they shelled those villages non-stop, using all artillery available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these actual extremist Muslim villages you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, my village of Osmace was an extremist village for them, and they used some information that we had 5.000 Mujahedin soldiers and rifles. And I claim here that all we had was the 21 hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, I'm moving into a fairly large new area, so it might be better if we could stop there and either come back five minutes later or have the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem at all with us. So we'll have a break now of half an hour, and that means we'll start at 10 minutes past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I think, actually, we can now give an exhibit number to the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become D741.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, did you know a place called Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Kravica have any sort of reputation among Muslims from even before the war?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of all evil, the force of the Chetnik movement in the area and everything negative coming from the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and that area of Podrinje, was Kravica. That was the reputation it had before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any incidents from before the war which gave sustenance to that opinion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The inhabitants of Kravica were constantly being violent. They spread this violence even in peacetime in Bratunac and all over. In 1991, a group of them stopped a vehicle with Muslim passengers, four of them, and I believe two guys were killed and two wounded. That was in 1991, and they used automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- do you know a place called Glogova?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Glogova in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Glogova was a 100 per cent Muslim village, with about 700 houses. So two to three times bigger than the Serb village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it remain a Muslim village throughout 1992? Did it remain inhabited as a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of May 1992, the Serbs from the Kravica area ethnically cleansed the villages of Kravica, Sandici, Mandici, and they killed about 150 to 200 people and they torched more than 1.000 Muslim homes. And they pillaged everything, Muslim property and commodities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have a new exhibit which we'd like to pass up, which doesn't have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take you up on what you've just said, that it doesn't have an ERN number. Do you mean to say that this was not given to you by the Prosecution, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And we'll have an explanation from the witness in a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide this document to us when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for this list from the organisation of demobilised fighters of Srebrenica, and these relevant data is used by the group that is searching for the dead and the missing in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not going to dwell over-long with this document; obviously for our purposes, there's a specific interest in this document. According to this document, 414 people from Glogova were killed during the war in Bosnia. I want to ask you: Have you been able to establish from this list how many Muslims from Glogova were killed prior to January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I counted; I believe it was 159 killed before January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that also on this list there are names of Muslims from Magasici Franca, and Bratunac, who were also --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those gravitating towards Kravica. So these people were put on the list of Kravica. So they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises; did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- the interpreters haven't understood your -- the last part of your reply, Mr. Buric. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that about 159 or 160 inhabitants of the village of Glogova, Magasici, Bratunac, Sandici, Hranca, were killed before March 1993, and the units from Kravica are held responsible for that. Therefore, people from Kravica killed these Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. I think we need to verify this. The witness said earlier on, page 42, line 1, page 42, line 1 to 4, "I asked for this list from the organisation of demobilised fighters of Srebrenica and these relevant data is used by the group that is searching for the dead and the missing in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What I would like to know is whether the lists that we have here includes also the names of dead persons whose body has been recovered, or not, or whether they are missing and their bodies still missing, too. Yes, Mr. Buric. Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said those who were killed and went missing. So next to each of the names, there should be a remark, "killed" or "missing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, because we don't have the English translation. What would be -- what would be the name -- the word for "missing" in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. No. No. In this table, there is no such a column, "missing" or "dead." I can't say which one of them was killed or which one went missing, but these are the two categories that the list pertains to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is [B/C/S spoken]? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You ask whether it was identified. I don't know. A part of them were buried and a part of them are still missing or in one of the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Place missing means unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, what's [B/C/S spoken], what does it mean, [B/C/S spoken]? If the interpreters could tell me what ---

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Occupation, profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means the type of schooling they completed and what their occupation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the response to your question, whether a person was killed or missing and whether that person has been identified. This is the place when -- where a person disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Look, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the last page should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I didn't notice that. Yes, we do have that in English. Place of missing, yeah, job, year of missing. All right. MR.
