DI FAZIO: Your Honour, this is just one matter that I haven't followed, and perhaps I misunderstood. The witness said in his evidence, he was talking about 159, 160 people from Glogova, missing or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I asked my question precisely because if they are just missing, it means one thing. If it includes also the dead that have been known to have been killed but their body was recovered, it's another. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that. My question is actually related to that. It's a different matter. The witness also went on to say -- it's gone off the screen now, but he said there were people killed from Kravica, and I don't know if there's anything in this document that shows that these 159 or 160 were killed by -- from people at Kravica. And I just wondered if I had misunderstood the evidence or -- I don't know how the document shows or illustrates how 159 people from that place were killed by people from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding is his evidence is that those from Kravica were responsible. The document itself doesn't speak to that. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Thank you. That's clarified things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be given Defence Exhibit number D742. Yes, Judge Eser has a question to the witness, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for the matter of clarification: There are two numbers on our screen, one saying 414 people from Glogova were killed during the war in Bosnia, and later, I think 159, prior to January 1993. So does it mean that the smaller number have been those people before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. January, and all the other ones have been killed later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding. I can clarify perhaps through the witness a couple of points in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned how the village of Glogova was ethnically cleansed, I think you said in May 1992. What's your understanding of how many Muslims were killed then, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking of the 9th of May, I think, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th or the 10th of May, I believe about 159 people. The Muslim villages around Kravica, Sandici, Mandici, Glogova, and Bratunac. So these people were killed directly by the units from Kravica until the 7th of May of 1993. 159 people killed or taken away and never heard of again. And the bodies were never buried. So killed or missing, until May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you saying 7th of May 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1992? Because Glogova wasn't attacked by the Serbs on the 9th of May of 1993, but on the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of Glogova was in Muslim hands throughout the war. So not the entire Glogova fell. In May of 1992, the Serbs torched a part of Glogova. And all the way until March of 1993, a part of Glogova was held -- was still in the hands of a group of people from Glogova itself. Q.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That leads on to the next topic. This group of people from Glogova itself who were still present in Glogova, did they have anyone who was a sort of leader or chief of that group?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boss of the Glogova group was Ejub Golic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for other people from Glogova, you've mentioned how a great many were killed in May 1992. Do you know, have any information about where the rest of the people from Glogova went? Did they all go to one place or did they go to various places?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first half of May of 1992, most of Glogova was torched by the Serbs, around 700 houses, and they killed most of the population of Glogova. The remaining inhabitants withdrew into the woods, to the western part of Glogova, to Bljeceva, Pale, and towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Kravica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there because a guy came along to see us and he asked my group to help. He said that Ejub entered, or rather, cut the communication lines between Bratunac and Kravica and that he didn't want to withdraw and he asked my group to come and help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that? What date?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 5th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he get this message to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came himself, this man from Glogova came to Osmace, and he told us what the matter was and he said would we come, and I gathered a group of about 40 to 50 lads, and most of them had arms, and we went in the direction of Pale, that is to say, Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said "this man from Glogova," do you mean Ejub Golic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know exactly what his family name is. I think his name was Kadir Music. Kadir is his first name, I'm positive about that. So he himself came and asked us to go and he took us to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he reach you? Do you know how he came to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that stage some kind of access to Osmace and Srebrenica did exist at that time. I think either on foot or by a lorry. I don't know. But he did walk to Osmace himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he walked to Osmace from Glogova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Osmace, yes, from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did you -- I'm not sure if you told us. Did you decide to give help to Ejub? In fact, sorry. Yes, you've told us you did. And you went in the direction of Pale. Where precisely did you go? And you can mark it on the map, if you can find it.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the new map, the small map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The new map. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could start by circling Kravica for us.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can circle Kravica, and this is Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the whole of Glogova or just a part of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova is a larger area. It is larger than what I've marked. As I said, there were more than 700 houses in Glogova. So they had quite a few hamlets. I don't remember all the names. But the entire area is called Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 5th of January, 1993, I believe, when did you actually arrive in the Kravica area? What date and what time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. At some point in the evening, we got to the area after Avdagine Njive at around 10.00 or 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you got there, you and your -- you and your lads?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a house, an improvised house, in fact, as it had been torched. Well, anyway, it was an improvised shelter. And so we sat down there. There was some hay thrown into that torched house. And that's where we spent the night. We stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the night of which day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What did you do the next day, on the 6th of January?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of January, we entered a Muslim village, a part of Avdagine Njive in the direction of Glogova. So we managed to sneak in from that direction. A part of Avdagine Njive which was in the direction of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you on that occasion speak to Ejub Golic or any of his group about what had been happening in that area in the previous weeks?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Ejub, in fact. Some lads came along and, for the most part, we were told by Kadir what the matter was, the fact that that communication line had been cut - I don't know on what date - and that they could no longer stand the attacks from the direction of Bratunac and from the direction of Kravica. And apparently thousands of shells were landing upon them on a daily basis, and infantry weapons were also fired at them. And so that was our main aim, to go and help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you've referred to these attacks from the direction of Bratunac and from the direction of Kravica. Do you know when that had been happening? Was that in the days before or the weeks before? When did you understand that had been going on?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for weeks before. The way I understood it was for weeks on end. For weeks, Serbs were shelling that area of Glogova incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness a couple of new exhibits. One is ERN 04363028. And while it's being distributed, it's Bratunac Brigade command, strictly confidential number 882-92, date 10 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. While this is being done, Mr. Jones, perhaps Mr. Buric can tell us: This person that came to seek your help from Glogova, and you said he walked all the way to Osmace, what would be the distance that he would have covered on foot? How many kilometres? Because it's quite a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite clear in what I said. I said that he walked to Osmace. There is an asphalt road of two kilometres where there was no link. So I suppose he must have reached that asphalt road via truck. And between the two, it wasn't possible for a truck to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I've misunderstood that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could perhaps clarify this. There is a distance of 18 kilometres between Osmace and Srebrenica. Below Osmace, there is an asphalt road, and so Osmace to Srebrenica is 18 kilometres. But as of that asphalt road, to go to Osmace, there is a path of two kilometres where you can't drive, you can't go down that road by a truck. So I suppose he must have been driven to that country road and then walked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing. Did Kadir also come from Srebrenica or did he come from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said from Glogova before. What I'm understanding is from Glogova he probably got a lift or something and then he walked it. This is what I can gather. Because I mean looking at the map itself, Osmace does not even show up on this map. And if there is a distance of 18 kilometres between Osmace and Srebrenica, and then you look at the distance on the map at least between Srebrenica and Glogova, it's quite a distance. We're talking of over 40 kilometres, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be correct. And I think from the witness's answer, possible conveyance by truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not arguing that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine for my purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see this document, Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make sure that we're talking of the same one, since you mentioned two. This is the one with ERN 04363028.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's it, yes. And it's to Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you see the second bullet point: "I have relocated part of the units to the Kravica area. I'm carrying out preparations according to your order." This is dated 10 December 1992, to the Drina Corps command, and signed Lieutenant Colonel Borivoje Tesic. My question is. Did you have information to the effect that there was increased activity in Kravica in December 1992, increased military activity on the part of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were on our way, Kadir told us that in the Kravica area, reinforcements were arriving on a daily basis from Bratunac and Bijeljina and that there were special units that the Tigers, led by Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. And apart from the battalion that we knew existed in Kravica, they also kept receiving assistance from other Serb units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd just ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, which is, as I said, has in the original language ERN number 04363028, with the corresponding English translation accompanying it, is being given Defence Exhibit number D743.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll now pass to the next new exhibit, which is 04363034. And again, just while it's being distributed, it's Bratunac Brigade command, strictly confidential number 93/2-92, date 13 December 1992. It's to the command of the Drina Corps. And again, it's signed Lieutenant Colonel - and I think it's still Borivoje Tesic. In the English, that's come out as Dobrivoje but in the English we see Borivoje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, I want to ask you about 5 there, bullet point 5: "In the evening, over 2.000 citizens of Bratunac organised a welcome party for the men from Krajina." First I want to ask you what you would understand by the reference to that, the men from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said in the same way as Mauzer used to come from Bijeljina, the special units from Serbia and from Krajina kept coming to the area of Srebrenica non-stop, to the battlefields in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then moving on to paragraph 8: "After questioning those who have been captured, we may expect an attack on some of the positions on the Bratunac-Kravica road in order to thwart our action and cut off our troops. I've been undertaking measures to further reinforce the lines in the sector of the Glogova" -- it says "SM" -- and the Jezestica village SM. Everything else is going to plan." Now, I'll ask you first if you could actually locate Jezestica on the map, since that hasn't been located yet. And I'm going to ask you this: When you were -- when you arrived in the Kravica area, did you reconnoitre at all the lines? Did you establish where the division was between the Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We mentioned that on the 6th we checked the lines out and we could see that there was something going on there. Because as soon as we saw some kind of joy at capturing us, when they were celebrating, so to say, they would spend hours shelling the area of Glogova or some other area. And during those days they were bombing Srebrenica. They had planes involved as well, the air force, that is. So that was just the continuation of their offensive, which was initiated in November and December in that area. And we could see, since it was Christmas Day, for them in the morning, they were getting drunk, they were celebrating. And from the centre of Kravica, they were shooting at us using all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of questions about that. When you say "it was Christmas for them, in the morning," do you mean that morning, the 6th of January, 1993, or the following morning?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 7th of January, the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you've referred to shooting, shooting from Kravica. When was that occurring?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of January. In other words, they employed all available artillery. Not in any selective way along the battle lines, but they were shelling parts of Bljeceva, Glogova, they were shelling Paleceznici [phoen] and Potocari. Also the air force was used to bomb Srebrenica on the 6th. They were trying to draw our attention to the fact that Christmas was approaching, that they were celebrating. So it was active shelling. And since I myself was in the part of Avdagine Njive, the part where we were, my lads and I, we could see quite clearly, we had good visibility and we could see they were using tanks, Howitzers, and mortars. They must have been drunk and therefore they did not select their targets at all. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number fourth document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become D744, and Judge Eser --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I can ask later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ask it now. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before we leave the map, since we had problems to identify the way which Kadir took to come to Osmace, did I understand you correctly that you went back with Kadir to Glogova or Kravica? And if so, could you perhaps tell us which route you took from Osmace to Glogova, or Kravica, respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We went by truck from Osmace, and we got to Srebrenica. And from Srebrenica, we went on to Milicevici. From Milicevici we walked across Bljeceva to the sector which was called Avdagine Njive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark Avdagine Njive sector on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it very well, but here I've just marked it. This is an elevation. It is a Muslim village next to Kajici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you mark Kajici as well, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that Ejub Golic had actually, I think you said, disrupted the communications on the Kravica-Bratunac road. Where did he disrupt those communications, or disrupt that road?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He managed to do that in the other part, in the direction of Bratunac, between Glogova and Hranca. I said that when we got there, we did not see Ejub. We actually did not see Ejub at all. Throughout our stay at Glogova we did not see Ejub Golic. He was in the other part of the area, in the direction of Bratunac. But this was the road. In the direction of Hranici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps for later we should mark that. Perhaps you could put "EG" next to it to indicate that was where Golic severed the communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you in fact go into Kravica itself, the centre of Kravica, at any stage?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We entered Kravica on the 7th of January, between 10.00 and 11.00 on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many were in your group?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 50 lads in my group. And during the night, we were joined by the lads from Miholjevine, Mosici, Delici, led by Mefail nicknamed Zis. I can't remember what his family was. This Mefail was from the village of Zanjevo. But I don't know his family name. We all knew him by his nickname, Zis. So this was as we were going from Kajici to Kravica. There was this group from Osmace, and Mosici, Miholjevine, Jagodnja, and Joseva, those lads were there. And they came to the area independently of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned from -- was it in Mihajlovice or Miholjevine?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miholjevine. So that's at the elevation called Biljeg. That's where they had their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask what municipality that village is in.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the municipality of Srebrenica. You have Jagodnja, Joseva, and then Miholjevine. As far as I can remember, the elevation is 688.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a group from Zanjevo. What municipality is Zanjevo in?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zanjevo is in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned how, on the 6th already there were shooting from Kravica. Was that still going on on the 7th of January, 1993, or had it stopped?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They kept shelling from the direction of Kravica, because they knew that Ejub was in the area of Glogova. So it was not a selective shelling from Srupovo Brdo [phoen], Nemici, Bratunac, and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could just tell us where, on the 7th of January, just briefly, where you went and what you did, you and your group.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we checked out the lines on the 6th of January, we realised that there wasn't a whole lot of people along those lines and that they had already started their celebrations. And we were looking for the most adequate moment for us to check out what they were doing. And in the morning hours, that is to say, at 10.00, at around 10.00, we entered the Serb village of Kajici, where there wasn't all that much shooting. But then all available means were used to start firing upon us from Kravica. To the right of Kajici, there was a four-barrelled Flak gun, a Serb weapon, which was used to protect all the communication lines. So we found it very difficult to move in the direction of Kravica. There was a tank in the middle of Kravica itself that was protecting the valley from Avdagine Njive and the access to Kajici. And we are going down this road, and to the right, there is Hrastova Suma [phoen]. To my right, there was a group with Mefail and they managed to neutralise this Flak weapon, this big gun. And we managed to gain access to the village of Kravica and we entered the centre of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go through a few parts of what you just told us. Firstly, you said that you realised there wasn't a whole lot of people along those lines when you checked out the lines the day before. Are you talking about the whole of the defence lines in Kravica or is it some part of those lines where you found that there were not a whole lot of people?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am referring to the road leading to Kajici, in the direction that I was going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you've referred to a tank. Do you know what sort of tank it was?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. North of Kravica, all villages are Serb villages in the direction of Zelinja, Polom and the northern part towards the River Drina, and they had made a road and there was a T-55 tank. And as we were approaching Kravica, we could see that there was an APC as well, where they were withdrawing to the north, in the direction of Polom. I think they crossed Polom to the north, or else Zelinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this road. You say they had made a road and there was a T-55 tank. Can you tell us a bit more about this road, what sort of a road it was and why it was made, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that just before the war, and that means by the end of 1991/the beginning of 1992, they opened that road for a certain purpose, for that particular place. Since Kravica was situated between the Muslim villages of Glogova and Konjevic Polje. And they wanted to have a road of their own. And at Polom there was a pontoon bridge to cross the River Drina and get to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If you could locate Polom for us, please, on the map. Could you just circle Polom for me on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Polom or Zelinja. In that area. I'm not sure. But they were going north, either taking the road to Polom or Zelinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it necessary for there to be an access road to the Drina?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when a ban was imposed on any assistance coming from Serbia, so as not to have to use the Ljubovija bridge, they built a pontoon bridge at Polom, and all the units moved across that bridge at Polom. That was the best link they had, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us where the tank and the APC which you've referred to, roughly where you saw them on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll mark the place where the tank was with a "T." In the centre, there was the tank. And behind it was an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they stay there all through the 7th of January, 1993, or did they change location?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they saw us entering Kravica and they were unable to offer resistance, the tank and the APC and their population went northwards, across the hill, towards Polom and Zelinja. And what they couldn't take with them, they mined, or burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've marked on the map two arrows going to Zelinja and to Polom, I think you're indicating that you weren't quite sure where the road went, whether it went to the right or to the left. Is it right, in any event, that that road was going through the hamlets of Kravica, in the hills? I see one arrow goes near Ocenovici the other Celakovici [phoen]. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe towards Polom. I also marked the pontoon bridge. So that was the communication. I believe they went towards Polom. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The witness said that, talking about what he saw upon his entering into Kravica and people being unable to offer resistance, and said: "The population went northwards across the hill towards this place Polom." Then he said: "What they couldn't take with them, they mined or burned down." That's just incomprehensible. Are they talking about furniture, houses, where, what was mined, what was burned down? I know it's a matter for cross-examination, but I don't want to spend all my cross-examination clarifying matters that can very, very simply be clarified. And I respectfully suggest that this matter ought to be clarified. And although I may not be able to compel Mr. Jones to clarify that, I would invite the Trial Chamber to clarify the situation if Mr. Jones is unwilling to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm approaching it step by step. I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify that for us, please, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the time next to the tank was a Praga. I believe it's a 14-millimetre gun, mounted on an armoured vehicle. And it probably wasn't moving about, for some reason. When we entered Kravica, they managed to set that Praga on fire and it was still burning when they came in. They were unable to take it with them. It was there on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That deals only with one item. I think I would invite separate -- the objects that were mined because they couldn't take them with them, and the other objects or things that they set on fire. And if we divide the two, keep them separate, we'll get a better idea of what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with what was burned, this Praga. Can you explain for us what a Praga is, what calibre and anything else which would help us.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the tank and the APC went northwards behind the hills, so it wasn't destroyed in Kravica itself. And when the Serbs were retreating, I guess that vehicle malfunctioned and didn't want that to leave behind for us, and they set it on fire. They set that Praga on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll take this step by step. That's one item. Are there any other things which you saw which had been set on fire by the Serbs, which to your knowledge had been set on fire by the Serbs as they retreated?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on the left, in the centre of Kravica, next to the supermarket, there was a building, I believe a building of the farmers' cooperative, and it was mined. My group went in, and they demined the building and we seized large amounts and it was mined heavily, and we also seized a lot of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to come to that. You've given an example of one thing which was set on fire by the Serbs, one building which was mined. For my purposes, that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's sufficient, let's move, provided that Mr. Di Fazio is happy with it too. I suppose you are. Yes. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Other examples may come as we go along, but I don't want to spend too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling us about this warehouse - or sorry - this building where you seized large amounts, a lot of weapons. Can you tell us as precisely as possible what you captured there.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Kravica, there was the building next to the old supermarket. I believe that was the building of the farmers' cooperative and the warehouse. And when we came in, we saw it was mined. The guys demined it. They cut the cables. And we saw a large number of crates with weapons. My group seized exactly 96 light machine-guns, or automatic rifles; 11 semi-automatic rifles; large quantities of ammunition. We found two mortars that they used for shelling in the centre of Kravica. There were lots of crates of grenades. We found Serb olive-drab uniforms. I don't know how many exactly, but a lot. They were neatly folded there. And on the right side of the warehouse, the Praga was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And either then or later, did you learn whether this was all that was seized from Kravica, or were other weapons and ammunition seized that day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In every house, there were at least two to three pieces of weaponry. We found great quantities of arms when the houses were searched. We found a lot of automatic rifles, light machine-guns, ammunition, equipment, all in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to clarify a couple of other matters. What time of day was it when you went into Kravica, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps between 12.00 and 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at one point you referred to there not being much resistance from the Serbs in Kravica. Do I understand from that that you weren't -- you and your group weren't shot upon in any way, that you walked into Kravica without any resistance, or was it otherwise?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said in Kajici there was no significant resistance, because they withdrew to Kravica and they were celebrating. Because we found food, lambs on the spit, pigs, and we caught them by surprise, until we reached the centre of Kravica. By that time they had realised what was happening and then they returned fire from everything they had. But they held the exit towards Polom and Zelinja. It was their route to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that then they returned fire from everything they had. Can you tell us where they were shooting from? What places or objects they were returning fire from?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all of the houses. They fired from all of the houses that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've mentioned finding ammunition and arms when houses were searched. Did you go into many houses in Kravica once the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. action was over?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came out of the warehouse, two or three guys stayed behind on the left side, and I came into the house that was on the right, and that was an outpatient clinic close to the warehouse and we seized a lot medication there, because there was a great need for that in Srebrenica. Srebrenica was not only short of food, but any sort of medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not a house. That's a building. The question -- I appreciate it's important, but Mr. Jones asked you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A house. It was a house that they used as a pharmacy. A house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you enter other houses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three, max.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I speak for myself personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did any of the men in your group go into houses, other houses, apart from the ones you went into?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a portion of the houses, because we were informed, perhaps around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m., that we urgently needed to go back. Because Kragljivoda was under attack and the lines of defence were in danger and they have issued an offensive. We had no further time to stay there. We had to come together again and go back to the area of Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then since you went into only two or three houses, on what basis do you say that in every house there were weapons and arms and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard from others that they found large amounts of arms. That was not the only depot. There were other locations where they found equipment and arms. That was not the only depot. We heard that later. And most of the weaponry was given to Biljeg, Glogova, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask if the witness could be shown D469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could have a look at that document, please. It's to the Drina Corps Command, date 9 January, 1993. And I'll read the top paragraph: "In the course of combat between the hours of 0830 and 1800 on 7 January, 1993, during the withdrawal of the 3rd Kravica PB, infantry battalion, the following MTS, materiel, and technical equipment was left behind in Kravica." And then we see a list of 25 items. And then under "B," we see six items which were allegedly destroyed. I'll ask you, Mr. Buric, to look very carefully down this list, and wherever possible, to provide a comment on what's referred to there in light of your experience in Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993. So if you can go to one, vehicle, T-1, if that's something you can confirm, two, Mercedes. You see what I mean. If you would please do that.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the Praga was set on fire, that was the Mercedes, where it says "armoured." That was the vehicle that was set on fire. People found a lot of their own tractors and trucks that the Serbs had seized from the Muslim villages of Bratunac and Glogova previously, when they plundered them in May of 1992. They found a lot of their own vehicles and machinery in Kravica. I don't remember the exact names of the vehicles, but I know there were a lot of passenger vehicles of Zastava and Niva. But most of it was taken in the fields and set on fire. I mentioned what was seized by my group, but I wasn't very familiar with what it was that the other groups seized. But I do know that a lot of weaponry was found, as well as mines and grenades. And if I may conclude what I was personally surprised with was something that I couldn't forget. It was in the warehouse. I saw large quantities of oil. These were canisters of 25 litres each and it said "the US of A." This was American oil received as part of the humanitarian aid that was intended for the convoy in Srebrenica in February. So there were tonnes of that oil. They took it and used it for their own military purposes, for their battalion, instead of giving it to the people as aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to 8 and 9, which refers to shells, 60-millimetre mortar shells and shells for the ZIS. Is that something you can comment on, as to whether that was captured on that day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four-barrelled gun was on the right, and seized. That was the one that I saw. And in the centre itself, there was an 82- and 60-millimetre mortar, perhaps two or three of them, actually. I don't remember exactly. I didn't see the three-barrelled gun, but I suppose there were units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 8 and 9, were you aware of any shells being captured?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, there were a lot of shells for mortars and guns, as well as several Zoljas, hand-held rocket launchers and the shells for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned three -- four-barrelled gun. We see under "destroyed," number two, three barrelled, and then it says "from Bijeljina." Now, you referred to units from Bijeljina and Kravica. Do you know at all what this refers to? Is it something you can enlighten us on?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in the area of Bratunac and Srebrenica, there was always the unit of Ljubisa Savic [phoen], called Mauzer, from Bijeljina, and they came to their aid, as well as some reserve forces from Serbia. So I guess that three-barrelled gun belonged to them. I didn't see that, but I did see the four-barrelled gun. It stayed back in Kajici, on one of the hills to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about number 4, the ZIS gun? Do you know what that refers to? And if so, did you see it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a gun of 76-millimetre calibre, as well as 75. It stayed behind. I didn't see it, but it must have been in the area somewhere. It wasn't on my axis of movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it would actually help just as a visual aid to look at the photographs, just so we know a little bit of what we're talking about. We're not all experts on artillery or tanks. So I'd ask if this new exhibit could be distributed. It's marked at the top "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, agreement on confidence and security-building measures in Bosnia-Herzegovina, photographic exchange." This is just an extract, I should say. I should also say the pages aren't numbered. I've numbered them myself, from battle tanks on page 1, through the rest. Mr. Buric, I'm just going to ask you to look at these photographs and provide me any commentary. Firstly, is that page 1? Does it say "battle tanks at the top? Yes. You told us that you saw a T-55 tank. Is that something like what you saw in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, we have 82-millimetre mortar. We see on the list, D469 under "destroyed," 82-millimetre mortars. Did you see mortars of this calibre in Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I saw two or three pieces that were ready for firing on the lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And next we have an anti-tank gun, 75-millimetre. Did you see something like that in Kravica? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a recoilless gun that they used expansively, and they used to mount them on APCs. On Serb APCs one could find two such recoilless guns. It was an alteration they made, and they usually mounted them on APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've referred to APCs in Kravica on that day. Did they have mounted guns or were they without any weaponry?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see it, but I presume that the anti-aircraft machine-gun was on it, the PAM, of 12.7-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you presume that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A larger-calibre gun sounded differently, so we knew what we were being shot at from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next page we see type M-42 ZIS gun, 76 millimetres. Is that, or is it not, something similar to the ZIS gun which you've referred to in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that on my axis I didn't see such a weaponry. But this is a ZIS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come across any shells for a ZIS when you were in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. It was in the crates. And when it was taken out of the storage, we saw that there were shells, but we didn't know whether they were for a launcher or a tank or a ZIS or a gun. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number, please, for this photograph exhibit. I won't go into the machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this will become Defence Exhibit 745. And for the record, it does not have an ERN. It does not have an ERN number. And it consists of a front page, which describes the nature of the document, the entire document, states "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, agreement on confidence and security-building measures in Bosnia and Herzegovina, photographic exchange, according to measures 1 ...", paragraph 2, and this is supposed to be in the English language, which it is. Date of exchange being indicated as the 1st of April of 1998. The same document is then followed by seven pages, on which are shown various kinds of artillery and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this tank and transporter, I just want to stay with it a bit longer. I think you said they withdrew along this mountain road towards the Drina. One or two, the tank and APC, was there any shooting or were the guns silent as they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time that I was in the area, the tank and the APC fired from that area, and the other pieces that came to their aid from Bratunac, they were shooting from that side of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the projectiles landing? Where were they shooting into?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shooting at the centre of Kravica. They withdrew, and thousands of Muslims came into the house. They were collecting food. They came from the direction of Glogova. There were several thousand of them. And anything that moved, they shelled. So the very centre of Kravica, one house at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you described for us how in Fakovici there were thousands of Muslim civilians. Rather than going into this subject again in great detail, was there any significance difference between the situation of civilians in and among the houses looking for food in Fakovici and the scenes you saw in Kravica? Were there fewer civilians, were there more civilians?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the short period of time that we were in Kravica, I can claim with full responsibility that if in Fakovici there were 10.000 to 15.000 civilians, in Kravica there were between 20.000 to 30.000 civilians, in my estimate. They were civilians. And when we were going back, we encountered groups of people moving towards Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And it may be [inaudible] to you, if the Prosecution puts their case to you, it may be suggested to you or asked of you: Why didn't fighters link arm in arm and form a giant cordon and keep these people out, or somehow stop the civilians from entering and possibly causing some damage to Serb property?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great mass of people. And as I said, the only reason for such great numbers to move towards Kravica was food, and only food. There was no intention of revenge or anything else. The only reason for those civilians to enter Kravica was to find food and to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you weren't going to go and stop them surviving?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- we didn't want to. We weren't able to, and nobody else in this whole wide world would have been able to stop them. There's nothing you can do to stop a hungry person looking for food. If a person is starving, dying of thirst and hunger, they will go to the first shop or to the first hotel and steal some food, and in this case they went to the first Serb house and got some food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one important correction to the transcript. The witness said, "It's not that we didn't want to prevent them, but we could not stop them." And it went like, "We did not want to." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are correct. Nobody could, nobody was in a position to do that. Even if you had lots of armed people, they would not have been able to prevent people going to get food. The only reason they moved was a sheer fight for survival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. And thank you, Mr. Buric. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see on that day, 7th of January, 1993, when you were there in Kravica, anyone deliberately setting fire to houses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I did not see it. And nothing was on fire. I mean, we were there for three or four hours, and not a single house was on fire in the direction that I was going in. And we went back the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were obviously in one part of this area of Kravica. Were you aware of fighting going on in any other part of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard shooting from all sides. That shooting was probably meant for us, those of us who were entering Kravica were being shot at from all sides. That was the impression we had when we were in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a place called Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours would give me a moment. Yes, I'm actually going to move on to another area altogether, Mr. Buric, and we may return to the first map, but it's a subject I intend to take briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- you mentioned a place, Jezero, frequently yesterday. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us a lot about the situation in Jezero in 1992. I'm interested in Jezero in January 1993. So I want you to cast your mind back to January 1993 and Jezero. And tell us, please, whether what you've described in relation to Jezero in 1992, in terms of artillery and units placed there, whether that was the same position in January 1993 or whether it had changed in any way, to your knowledge. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, what Kravica meant to the Muslim people in the municipality of Bratunac, that was Jezero for the municipality of Srebrenica. In the area of Jezero, there were about ten Muslim houses, and one or two Serb houses. In April and May 1992, the Serbs took those houses and then placed their artillery there. And throughout that period, between April and March, the main shelling was coming from Jezero. Let me clarify this once again. They had a wire perimeter, and then there were land-mines, and the artillery was within that perimeter, and they were still not feeling safe enough. And five or six kilometres away, they did the same, in a village called Kusici. They had their artillery weapons, guns, and tanks. And they were getting regular assistance from Serbia, from Tara and Perucac. Shall I marked Kusici on the map? So Kusici is not marked here, but it's a road. And there were one or two Serb houses; I'm not sure. And at that plateau they placed Howitzers and guns. And they kept shelling the entire area of Srebrenica 24 hours a day, non-stop and I'm referring to the area of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that position, that situation that you've described, was that true in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had already established some links amongst the territories by the end of 1993, and this constant destruction and shelling, with all sorts of weapons, could no longer be tolerated. And as time went on, Serbs started using ever more state-of-the-art weapons. And in January, I think around the 15th or the 16th of January, they -- a decision was made to attack their artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was going to ask you. And did you participate in that attack on their artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in the direction of Kragljivoda, Jezero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Just a minor matter. I think -- I don't know, but I think a correction might be required. The witness said "we established some links among the territories by the end of 1993." That's what it says in the transcript. I don't know if that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I only heard the translation. MR. DI FAZIO: Right. Well, I wonder if that's what the witness said or whether he meant to say 1992. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's probably correct. Mr. Buric I'm surely can help with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993. I'm referring to 1993, in fact. In January 1993, some territory was broadened, enlarged, at around Osmace, Karacici, Kragljivoda, Poznanovici, Miholjevine, and there were no longer any Serb patrols in the way. And following that, we decided to deal with Jezero, which was the main problem for all those territories. So the transcript was in fact correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, in fact, what you're telling us is this: By the end of 1992, you had managed to link up, because these patrols weren't continuing. And therefore, by January 1993 --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you unhappy with that, Mr. Di Fazio, or -- because it sort of contradicts what he said in the previous -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. The clarification was there and it was January 1993, not the end of 1992. January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand it throughout that he means that this line of communication was re-established by the end of 1992. So that the situation was crystallised in the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it to be, but that's not how he explained it at one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that at one point ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, you've heard what's been said. Can you --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually manage to take Jezero on the 16th, 15th or 16th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise about before. What I said was by the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, certain territories were linked up in that area, and that's why the decision was made on the 16th of January to attack this place called Jezero. However, we did not take it on the 16th of January, because we were unable to get across. I was attacking from the direction of Kragljivoda and Vitez. There was an asphalt road, and we were travelling down that road. And we left a way out for the Serbs to withdraw, in the direction of Jezero and Perucac. And that's what they did. I think it was the 19th or the 20th of January, the Serbs who were members of the battalion in Jezero, there were about 100 people there, and they withdrew. And we had informed them beforehand that they could get out in the direction of Perucac, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Did you capture anything in Jezero when it was -- when it finally fell?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say earlier: As they withdrew, there was about a dozen Muslim houses there which they were using as barracks, as warehouses for their weapons and artillery. In the early morning hours, at around 6.00 a.m. on the 19th and the 20th, they blew it all up. As they withdrew, they blew up those houses. I don't know how to explain this, but those were kinds of time bombs. So in the early morning hours, half 6.00, 6.00, it all went up. And all the artillery and the guns and cannons, they all threw things around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So in other words, you say there were some sort of timers or time bombs. And then after the Serbs had withdrawn, it all went up in a big, big explosion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that cause damage to property?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As I said, all those ten houses were destroyed, totally devastated by those explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened after Jezero fell? You mentioned Kusici. What was the situation there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Jezero, we went on to Kusici. And our units had entered a day or two earlier, I don't know, they had entered Kusici. And in the same way, as I said, at Kusici they had even more contemporary, state-of-the-art weapons, and they left a couple of guns or cannons, mortar, 120 millimetres, that was brought to the battleground for the first time. And then 60- and 80-millimetre mortars, and they all left it without any breeches. That was the stuff that they took with them as they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown D746. My apologies. I'm anticipating that it will be D746. I got ahead of myself. The ERN is 04367489. Sorry if that's presumptuous, that it will become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry. One day you'll make it, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the meantime, I'll just read the top portion: "Independent Battalion Skelani, strictly confidential, 24-1, date 7 January 1993, 1430 hours," and it refers to the deployment of minefields and firing positions of large calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, just that reference to the Independent Battalion command Skelani, and this is January 1993, did you have any information about how many Serb soldiers were present in Skelani in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information according to which the Skelani Battalion was a permanent fixture, and that they had a special Red Beret platoon as well, which was, as I said before, led by somebody called Zivko Policajac. I mentioned this yesterday. And according to needs, they were joined by units from the Uzice Corps. So depending on their needs, they would be joined by those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uzice Corps from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were volunteers from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We have the first paragraph referring to -- well, I'll read it into the record: "In the zone of responsibility of our unit we did not lay typical minefields, but groups of mines at the following locations." And then the locations are given. I want to concentrate on two artillery firing positions, feature 688, mixed artillery battery, 500-millimetre Howitzer, M-42 gun, 120-millimetre mortar, two pieces, 82-millimetre mortar. It refers to Ripa and then Cosici and then Jezero and Bujakovici. Now, are you familiar with these locations? You've told us about Jezero, but are you familiar with the other locations and can you confirm on the basis of your own experience whether there was artillery located there in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just correct you. There is no 500-millimetre weapon, but it must be something big. However, I can say the following: We did know for certain that there was artillery at Jezero, and they kept getting supports from Perucac and from the Tara plateau. And aircraft were taking off from Ponikve, and minefields, well, minefields are the continuation of the minefields from Fakovici, Radijevici, Boljevici, Kutijesi. And around Skelani, Cosici, and Jezero, everything was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then for those other positions, in Cosici, Bujakovici, and Orlov Vis, are you familiar with those places?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with Cosici, because around Cosici, everything was mined, and they had a professional company from Skelani that was stationed at Cosici all the time. My brother-in-law, Ramo Halilovic, was killed in the area of Cosici because he stepped on a land-mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's land-mines. How about artillery in Cosici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every Serb village had a mortar. Every single Serb village had an 82- and a 60-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that specifically for Cosici or that's based on a general observation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We knew it, that there were mortars in Cosici and that there were minefields around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Mehmedalija Tihic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, firstly, is he alive?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since there was a shortage of food, Mehmedalija used to go to his original area of Skelani two or three times a week. And when he left to get food last time, he stepped on a land-mine at Cosici, where he was slightly wounded, and then he was captured by the people at Skelani there. And he spent a long time in the prison in Skelani. And in 1993, at some point in March 1993, he simply went missing from Skelani. We lost all trace of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's never been heard of since?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing, not a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if this could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And as predicted by you, Mr. Jones, this will become Defence Exhibit D746.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Not an objection. I just wondered if anyone could indicate where Cosici is on the map. I was just trying to follow the evidence and I couldn't locate it. And I wondered if perhaps the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness is doing as directed. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps the witness might --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can try. This is Arapovici, Palkovici [phoen], Arapovici. Somewhere here, approximately here, Kostalonci [phoen]. I'm going to try and mark it here, roughly speaking, that's where Cosici should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've marked it with an "X," for the record.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I marked it with the letter "X."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to -- I'm very close to the end, Your Honours, but it may be I will need to go on ten minutes on Monday, and I don't want to rush things. So with your indulgence, I know I've gone over the original estimate, but more evidence has a emerged during proofing and in the course of his evidence. So I'll need another ten minutes on Monday, but I'll try to make as much progress now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've told you it's not going to be a problem. And looking at Mr. Di Fazio's eyes this morning, I think there won't be any problem on their side either. MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday and Tuesday, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll finish promptly, then, on one today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, I now want you to just describe briefly, Mr. Buric, what happened in Osmace after the events in Jezero in late January 1993. And if you could just explain what happened between January and March 1993.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the elevation, Jezero, was taken, as well as Kusici, total chaos broke out in the area of Osmace, Karacici, and Kragljivoda, those Muslim villages that were in the direction of Jezero. On a daily basis, there was shelling. I keep repeating this, but I feel I have to. From Skelani, from the Perucac-Jezero plateau, from Tara, and on a daily basis, aircraft were taking off from Bratunac. There were two planes that were called Komarac, mosquito, and they were bombing the villages, Osmace, Peracici [phoen] and Kragljivoda on a daily basis in that part of Jezero, once again, on a daily basis throughout January and February and March. In March, they interested the Uzice Corps from the direction of Skelani. So they had reinforcements, the Skelani Battalion had reinforcements, as well as the battalions from Bratunac and Bijeljina. The volunteers started an all-out offensive, together with the Serb volunteers, against the Muslim villages in the direction of Srebrenica. We are talking about a period of time between 20 and the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just one matter which might cause confusion later. You said Perucac-Jezero plateau. Am I right that Jezero in your language means "lake," as well as being the name of a place?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant the plateau -- the lake of Perucac, then. It is an area where there are hotels and a village next to the dam on this lake of Perucac. So that's what we refer to as "plateau."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It might help if you could just on the map circle Perucac. And while you're at it, if you can, Orlov Vis, which we saw in another document?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the hydroelectric powerplant. This is where the Bajina Basta powerplant is, Perucac. The road is not marked on the map, but it is being completed. It is an asphalt road. And at every turning, there was a Serb tank. I'm going to try, once again, and I apologise, but I'm going to try and show you this winding road. So at every turning, there was a tank. So there were about 15 to 20 tanks at all times, all over this plateau of the Perucac, of the lake of Perucac, and so this is the road from Perucac to Tara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you locate Orlov Vis on the map as well? Only if you're familiar with the location. If you're not, then don't worry.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it should go all the way to Bajina Basta, but I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not critical. I interrupted you when you were referring to they being bombed on a daily basis in Osmace and Kragljivoda. Did Osmace actually fall at some point?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, the lads who were from Osmace, we were in the sector of Kragljivoda. It's a distance of about seven kilometres from Osmace and we saw a column of vehicles. And people from my group actually counted them. There were 140 APCs, buses, tanks, a -- Niva cars, hospital vehicles. And in a long column of 140 of them, went in the direction of Jezero from Skelani, and those were those parts of the Uzice Corps, with the units from Skelani, from Jezero, who were coming back to that area. And they went on in the direction of Kragljivoda. And on the 23rd of March, they took Osmace. Osmace was an ethnically pure village, a Muslim village, not just Osmace, but Osat, Sedace, Radjenovic, and Klotjevac, and on the other side, Karacici. All that fell on the 23rd of March and there was an all-out Serb offensive on that day. So in that offensive they razed everything to the ground, they torched everything. First of all, they would loot the villages and then set them on fire. And that was evident afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Seeing the time, that would be a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect, Mr. Jones. Mr. Buric, we are going to stop here today, and we will resume your and your conclude your examination-in-chief on Monday. That will take us into Tuesday for sure to bring your examination to an end. I wish you all a good weekend. In the meantime, the witness is reminded you're not allowed to communicate or allow anyone to communicate with you on matters related to your evidence. It does not mean that you cannot communicate with your family and friends and whoever. I take this opportunity to thank not only the parties and my staff, but also the staff of the Registry, technicians, and interpreters and all the others, for having made it possible for us to finish at 1.00 today, reducing the sitting by about 15 minutes. Thank you.
